title: Metropolitan entanglement distribution between an atom and a near-visible photon
authors: Maya Büki, Pooja Malik, Florian Fertig, Tobias Frank, Marvin Scholz, Tommy Block, Gianvito Chiarella, Yiru Zhou, Emanuele Distante, Pau Farrera, Gerhard Rempe, Harald Weinfurter
abstract: Entanglement distribution is the overarching purpose of quantum networks. While communication over long distances can use deployed fiber infrastructure, it requires photons in the telecom band. However, advanced quantum network nodes do not operate at such wavelengths. Here we overcome this limitation with two tailor-made low-noise quantum-frequency converters to distribute entanglement between a single atom and a resonant photon over 14km line-of-sight via 24km of a deployed commercial fiber. The photon at wavelength 780nm is first entangled with the atom, then converted to the telecom S-band, and finally back-converted after propagation through the fiber. This link enables a photon transfer efficiency of 1.7% while affecting the atom-photon entanglement fidelity by less than 1%. This brings integration of atomic quantum nodes with existing long-distance fiber networks into reach, enabling novel applications in quantum information processing.
summary: The research demonstrates a functional metropolitan quantum network link by distributing entanglement between an atom and a photon over $24 	ext{ km}$ of standard optical fiber. This was achieved by employing specialized quantum frequency converters to shift the photon's wavelength between the atomic resonance (visible) and the telecom band. The success proves a crucial step toward integrating local quantum processors with existing long-distance communication infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the wavelength mismatch between quantum network nodes (operating at visible/near-visible wavelengths) and the telecom band required for long-distance fiber transmission to distribute entanglement.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a metropolitan quantum link capable of distributing atom-photon entanglement over 24 km by implementing bidirectional frequency conversion, maintaining high fidelity ($F \geq 86.9\%$).
method: The experiment utilizes quantum frequency converters (QFCs) based on periodically-poled lithium niobate to convert the photon wavelength between the atomic resonance ($\lambda = 780 	ext{ nm}$) and the telecom S-band ($	ext{1514 nm}$), enabling transmission through deployed fiber.
model_or_system: The system is a metropolitan quantum link connecting two laboratories via $24 	ext{ km}$ of commercial optical fiber. It involves an atomic qubit (e.g., $	ext{Rb}$) entangled with a photon, which undergoes conversion at the ends of the fiber segment.
key_observables: Entanglement fidelity ($F$), visibility ($ ar{V}$), Bell parameter ($S$), and overall entanglement distribution efficiency.
important_parameters: Fiber length ($24 	ext{ km}$), atomic wavelength ($780 	ext{ nm}$), telecom wavelength ($	ext{1514 nm}$), and achieved photon transfer efficiency ($1.7\%$).
main_assumptions: The system relies on the functionality of quantum frequency converters and assumes stable operation despite environmental drifts, which are actively corrected using classical polarization monitoring.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup showing entanglement generation at $780 	ext{ nm}$, conversion to $	ext{1514 nm}$ for fiber propagation, and back-conversion. Results show state correlations confirming entanglement violation of Bell's inequality both before and after full link transmission.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup involving frequency conversion stages ($	ext{QFC}1$ and $	ext{QFC}2$) to bridge wavelength gaps, followed by long-distance propagation through fiber. Key results confirm high fidelity entanglement distribution over $24 	ext{ km}$, concluding with a discussion of future applications in quantum networking.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the critical engineering hurdle—wavelength conversion—necessary to connect atomic quantum memories (which operate at visible wavelengths) with existing, long-haul fiber infrastructure used for quantum communication networks.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Metropolitan quantum link. Two laboratories in the greater Munich area are connected via a 24 km long fiber in order to distribute atom-photon entanglement. The Rb atom at LMU (node 1) is entangled with a photonic qubit (see level scheme) which is subsequently converted to a telecom wave- length at QFC1, propagates 24 km of fiber, is back-converted to 780 nm at QFC2, and after spectral filtering finally mea- sured in a photon projection measurement at MPQ (node 2). After communicating to LMU the arrival of the photon at MPQ, the atomic state is measured via florescence read- out using a micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) switch and an avalanche photodetector (APD).

FIG. 2. Characterization of the QFCs. Measurement of the external conversion efficiency of QFC1 (a) and QFC2 (b) - in red - and noise at the end of the communication link when changing (a) the pump power of QFC1 (power of QFC2 is fixed at 300 mW) and (b) the pump power of QFC2 (power of QFC1 is fixed at 400 mW) - in blue. The ratio between the ef- ficiency and the noise clicks is proportional to the SNR, which is depicted in green. All solid lines are obtained from fits to experimental data using equations that are found in [47]. The vertical dashed grey lines indicate the pump powers used in the entanglement experiment for QFC1 and QFC2 respec- tively.

FIG. 4. Atom-photon state correlation at 780 nm after 24 km of fiber. Conditional redetection probability of the atom at maximum correlation points measured in three different basis combinations for both the atom (X,Y and Z) and the pho- ton measurement. The horizontal axis indicates the photon qubit polarization measurement result. The different values obtained for the VH, DA and LR bases lead to an average visibility of ¯V = 82.5 ± 2.0%. The photon detection rate for this measurement was 0.7 min−1. Error bars represent one standard deviation.

FIG. 3. Atom-photon state correlation at the telecom wave- length after 24 km of fiber. The conditional redetection prob- ability for different readout angles of the atom depending on the measured polarization state of the photon (horizontal and vertical (|H⟩, |V ⟩) or diagonal and antidiagonal linear polar- ization (|D⟩, |A⟩) ) as indicated in the legend shows fringes with the average visibility ¯V = 82.4 ± 0.8%. The measure- ment points at 45° and 135° are used for calculating the S- parameter, with result S = 2.30±0.08, clearly violating Bell’s inequality. Error bars represent one standard deviation, and the photon-detection window was set to 60 ns.
